<!--
C0 §8 — an amendment is ratified by a human (L4), never by the engine and never
by the author of the code it would unblock.

**The law changes before the check does, never the reverse.** If a rule or probe
is what prompted this, that rule waits until this issue is resolved.
-->

## Standard

<!-- The id, if this changes an existing standard. "New" if this adds one. -->

## Current text

<!-- Quote it exactly. If this proposes a new standard, write "none — new". -->

## Proposed text

<!-- The exact wording to be ratified, including the anti-pattern it must carry.
A standard with no anti-pattern can never become evidence, so a proposal without
one is incomplete. -->

## What prompted this

<!-- The situation the corpus did not cover, or covered wrongly. A concrete case
beats a general concern: an amendment argued from a real event is reviewable. -->

## Consequences

<!-- What becomes easier, and what becomes harder. An amendment with no cost
listed has not been thought about — every constraint costs something. -->

**Easier:**

**Harder:**

## Cross-constitution conflicts

<!-- S10.31 — check this against the other constitutions before the review
period opens. Two standards with equal authority saying incompatible things is
the failure this section exists to catch. -->

## Is this lowering a bar?

<!-- Answer explicitly. An amendment that makes a failing check pass is the one
case that needs the most scrutiny, and the honest answer is sometimes yes —
a bar set wrongly should move. What is never acceptable is moving it *quietly*. -->

- [ ] This does not lower a bar to make something pass.
- [ ] This lowers a bar, and the reasoning is written above.
